reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / standard medical genetics references
clinicalPearls: Second most common autosomal trisomy after Down syndrome and associated with severe multisystem malformation
Recognisable features include severe growth restriction, a prominent occiput, small jaw, low-set malformed ears, and clenched hands with overlapping fingers
Rocker-bottom feet and a short sternum are characteristic musculoskeletal findings
Major congenital heart defects, especially septal defects, are present in most affected infants
Marked feeding difficulties, apnoea, and central nervous system malformations contribute to early mortality
Caused by an extra copy of chromosome 18, most often from meiotic nondisjunction and increasing with maternal age
Incidence is higher at conception than at birth because many affected pregnancies end in miscarriage or stillbirth
Mosaic and partial trisomy forms may produce milder and more variable phenotypes
reference.pathophysiology: Edwards syndrome is caused by the presence of an extra copy of chromosome 18, usually a full trisomy resulting from maternal meiotic nondisjunction, with risk rising with advancing maternal age. Less commonly it results from mosaicism or a partial trisomy from an unbalanced translocation. The excess genetic material disrupts normal development across multiple organ systems during embryogenesis, producing the characteristic pattern of growth restriction, craniofacial and limb anomalies, cardiac and renal malformations, and central nervous system defects. The severity of malformations, particularly cardiac and neurological, drives the very high perinatal and infant mortality.
additionalDifferentials: Other chromosomal or single-gene multiple malformation syndromes
additionalInvestigations: Karyotype or chromosomal microarray to confirm trisomy 18 and identify mosaicism or translocation
Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing including cell-free DNA and, if indicated, amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling
Renal and cranial imaging for associated malformations
Parental karyotyping if a translocation is found
redFlags: Life-threatening cardiac and respiratory compromise in the newborn period
Recurrent apnoea and feeding failure requiring goals-of-care discussion
Increased risk of certain embryonal tumours in longer-surviving children
Need for early, compassionate counselling given the high mortality and prognosis
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is poor, with most affected infants dying in the first weeks or months of life and only a small proportion surviving beyond the first year, typically with profound disability; mosaic forms may fare better.
pitfalls: Failing to confirm mosaicism, which alters prognosis and counselling
Not offering parents balanced information about survival and quality of life
Overlooking treatable comfort and feeding issues while planning care
Missing the diagnosis antenatally when screening is declined or equivocal
management: Establish goals of care with the family early, as prognosis is poor, offering either comfort-focused palliative care or, in selected cases, active management of specific anomalies
Provide supportive care for feeding difficulties with nasogastric or gastrostomy feeding, and manage apnoea and respiratory needs as agreed within the care plan
Assess congenital heart defects by echocardiography and consider cardiac surgery only in carefully selected infants after multidisciplinary discussion
Treat complications such as infections, seizures and gastro-oesophageal reflux symptomatically
Coordinate multidisciplinary support across neonatology, paediatric palliative care, cardiology and allied health
Confirm the diagnosis with karyotype or microarray, offer genetic counselling, and perform parental karyotyping if a translocation is identified to assess recurrence risk
